abstract: >
  `glmnet` is the de-facto regularized generalized linear model engine in
  R, but its interface is built around a pre-constructed design matrix
  and a response vector. The gap between this style and base R's
  `glm()` is a recurring source of friction in applied work — factor
  handling, complete-case filtering, train/test design-matrix
  consistency, and a single λ-selection rule all land on the caller.
  This paper introduces fbrglm, a lightweight formula-based wrapper
  around `glmnet`. It accepts `formula` and `data`, stores
  training-time factor levels and contrasts on the fit object, rebuilds
  the prediction-time design matrix consistently, reports complete-case
  filtering explicitly, and exposes the underlying `glmnet` /
  `cv.glmnet` objects for downstream use. The package accepts the same
  family argument surface as `glmnet` itself — character strings for
  `gaussian`, `binomial`, `poisson`, `cox`, `multinomial`, `mgaussian`,
  and GLM family objects such as `stats::Gamma(link = "log")` or
  `MASS::negative.binomial(theta = ...)`. Current scope is
  `infer = "none"`; honest post-selection inference and additional
  features are deferred to later milestones. A small reproducible
  benchmark suite compares fbrglm to raw `glmnet`, `glmnetUtils`, and a
  `parsnip` / `workflows` pipeline; in the family-wide parity sweep
  fbrglm reproduces raw `glmnet` predictions across all eight
  glmnet-compatible families tested.

# Introduction

Base R's `glm()` provides a familiar formula/data interface for
generalized linear models, automatic handling of factor predictors via
`model.matrix()`, complete-case filtering through `na.action`, and S3
methods (`print`, `summary`, `predict`, `coef`, `nobs`, `plot`) that
applied statisticians rely on. `glmnet` [@friedman2010glmnet;
@tay2023glmnetall] adds L1/L2 regularization to this family and is
extensively used in practice, but its API operates on a
caller-constructed design matrix `x` and response vector `y`. Several
ergonomic frictions follow.

**Factor handling** is delegated to the caller. A common failure mode
is that `model.matrix()` applied to a test data frame, in isolation,
produces fewer columns than the matrix that was used at fit time when
the test factor's levels are narrower than the training factor's,
leading to a runtime error from `glmnet::predict()`.

**Missingness** is not handled. Callers must filter rows themselves;
there is no built-in "N rows dropped" report.

**λ selection** is post-hoc on the `cv.glmnet` object
(`$lambda.min`, `$lambda.1se`) or hand-supplied; the wrapper code
needed to thread a single choice through fit, predict, and report is
rewritten everywhere.

A goal of fbrglm is to package these conveniences into a wrapper that
*feels like `glm()`* and otherwise stays out of the way: no new
modelling abstraction, no new pipe, no opinion on inference. fbrglm
explicitly does **not** replace the `glmnet` computational engine.
`glmnet` and `cv.glmnet` are called verbatim under the hood, and the
resulting objects are stored on the `fbrglm` return value for direct
access. What fbrglm standardises is the surrounding formula/data
workflow and the prediction-time reconstruction of the design matrix
from training-time terms, contrasts, and factor levels.

## Contributions

The contributions of this paper, and of the accompanying R package,
are:

- a `glm()`-like formula interface to `glmnet` for the full set of
  families `glmnet` itself accepts (six character strings plus
  arbitrary GLM family objects);
- prediction-time reconstruction and alignment of design matrices
  using training-time terms, contrasts, and factor levels, with
  zero-padding of any missing one-hot columns;
- explicit reporting of missing-row handling (`nobs_info`) and
  rank-deficiency diagnostics (`rank_info`);
- lightweight interoperability through accessors for the underlying
  `glmnet` and `cv.glmnet` objects (`as_glmnet()`, `as_cv_glmnet()`);
- a reproducible benchmark suite comparing fbrglm against raw
  `glmnet`, `glmnetUtils`, and a `parsnip` / `workflows` pipeline,
  released as a companion experiments repository.

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2
expands the motivating problems with small reproducible examples.
Section 3 places fbrglm against related software and gives a feature
comparison table. Section 4 details the package design and
implementation, including pseudocode for the fit and predict paths.
Section 5 covers family support. Section 6 walks through worked
examples. Sections 7 and 8 describe the benchmark design and present
the results. Section 9 documents the replication material. Sections 10
and 11 close with limitations and concluding remarks.

# Motivating problems

This section makes the frictions described above concrete with small
reproducible snippets. Every code block runs against the package and
base R; nothing here depends on the fbrglm experiments repository.

## Formula interfaces versus matrix interfaces

Base R's `glm()` consumes a formula and a data frame; the design matrix
is constructed implicitly. `glmnet` does not, because it predates the
modern R formula machinery and because keeping the API matrix-shaped
is appropriate for an optimization-heavy package. Concretely:

```{r demo-glm-glmnet, eval = FALSE}
glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + g, data = train, family = binomial())
glmnet(model.matrix(y ~ x1 + x2 + g, train)[, -1, drop = FALSE],
       train$y, family = "binomial", lambda = 0.05)
```

The user is responsible for the second-line transformation and for
remembering, at predict time, how it was performed. The fbrglm form
collapses this back to a single call that retains the `glm()`-style
ergonomics:

```{r demo-fbrglm, eval = FALSE}
fbrglm(y ~ x1 + x2 + g, data = train,
       family = "binomial", lambda = "fix", lambda_value = 0.05)
```

## Training / test design-matrix mismatch

The single most error-prone consequence of moving the design-matrix
work onto the caller is mismatch between the columns used at fit time
and the columns the user (perhaps a different one, six months later)
hands to `predict()`. The standard example is a factor whose
**levels** are narrower in the test data than they were in the
training data:

```{r demo-mismatch}
library(fbrglm)
set.seed(7)
train <- data.frame(
    y  = rbinom(80, 1, 0.5),
    x1 = rnorm(80),
    g  = factor(sample(c("A","B","C","D"), 80, replace = TRUE),
                levels = c("A","B","C","D"))
)
test <- data.frame(
    x1 = rnorm(10),
    g  = factor(sample(c("A","B"), 10, replace = TRUE),
                levels = c("A","B"))   # narrower than training
)
X_train <- model.matrix(y ~ x1 + g, train)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
X_test  <- model.matrix(~ x1 + g, test)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
c(train_ncol = ncol(X_train), test_ncol = ncol(X_test))
```

A naive call to `glmnet::predict()` on `X_test` after a fit on
`X_train` raises a runtime error because the column counts do not
agree. fbrglm avoids this case structurally by carrying the
training-time terms, contrasts, and factor levels on the fitted
object, re-encoding `newdata` through the same machinery, and padding
any column whose factor level the test data did not happen to exercise
with zeros (Section 4).

## Factor levels and contrasts

A related but more subtle hazard is that two test data frames built
from the same observations can produce different design matrices
depending on which factor levels happen to appear and on the active
`contrasts` setting. For repeated experiments and serialized models
this is a reproducibility problem more than a "what error did I get"
problem: the model may silently consume a design matrix it was not
trained on. fbrglm's response is to store `terms`, `xlevels`, and
`contrasts` on the fit object and to reuse them — there is no global
state involved at predict time.

## Complete-case filtering and reproducibility

`glmnet` does not perform `na.action`-style filtering. Two-step
workflows that filter outside the model (`complete.cases(df)`,
`drop_na()`, etc.) work, but they decouple the "how many rows were
dropped" question from the model object and tend to be reinvented in
every project. fbrglm runs `model.frame(..., na.action = na.omit)`
under the hood and exposes the counts on the fit object as
`nobs_info$n_total`, `nobs_info$n_dropped_missing`, and
`nobs_info$n_used`. A one-line message is also printed at fit time
so the drop is not silent.

## λ selection as part of the model object

`cv.glmnet` produces a `$lambda.min` and a `$lambda.1se` plus the
full path. The decision of *which* λ a downstream call should use is
made by the caller, often in another file, sometimes inconsistently
between the fit step, the predict step, and the summary step. fbrglm
collapses this into a single argument `lambda %in% c("cv_min",
"cv_1se", "fix")` and stores the resulting numeric λ as
`fit$lambda_value`. `print()`, `summary()`, `coef()`, `predict()`,
and `plot()` all dispatch from there.

## Why regularized GLMs complicate classical glm-style summaries

`summary.glm()` returns the IRLS-derived asymptotic standard errors
and z / p / CI quantities that statisticians routinely use. For a
regularized fit those quantities are *not* simply IRLS standard errors
of the regularized coefficients: the shrinkage introduces bias, the
selection of non-zero terms is data-dependent, and the asymptotic
calculations break in non-trivial ways. Honest post-selection
inference (data splitting, selective inference [@tibshirani2016selective]) is a substantial body of work. fbrglm's
position is to refuse to produce classical SE / z / p / CI under
`infer = "none"` rather than report numbers that look like the glm()
output but mean something different.

## Serialization and reuse across R sessions

A subtle reproducibility hazard with do-it-yourself
`model.matrix()` workflows is that the recipe used to build the
training design matrix is *not* part of the object the user saves
to disk. A typical pipeline writes out the `glmnet` object via
`saveRDS()`, brings it back next quarter, builds a new design matrix
from a fresh sample with `model.matrix(formula, newdata)[, -1, drop
= FALSE]`, and quietly hits a different layout: factor levels have
shifted, a previously-unused level now appears (or disappears),
`options("contrasts")` is different on the new machine, or the
original formula was lost. The result is either a sharp error or, in
the worst case, silent disagreement between training and serving.

fbrglm makes the recipe a first-class part of the saved object.
`terms`, `xlevels`, `contrasts`, and the literal training column
names live on the fit and are reused at predict time without
consulting global state. A serialized `fbrglm` object loaded into a
fresh R session reconstructs the same design matrix from the same
data, independently of session-level contrasts settings, factor
attribute defaults, or what other packages are attached.

# Related software

The R ecosystem already contains several packages that touch the gap
between `glm()`-style ergonomics and `glmnet`, with different scopes.

- **stats::glm** is the reference formula/data GLM interface in base R
  [@R] but does not provide regularization.
- **glmnet** [@friedman2010glmnet; @simon2011glmnetcox;
  @tay2023glmnetall] is the de-facto regularized GLM engine. fbrglm
  delegates all optimization to it.
- **glmnetUtils** [@glmnetUtils] provides `glmnet(formula, data)`
  and `cv.glmnet(formula, data)` wrappers and a predict path that
  accepts `newdata`. It is the closest alternative in spirit to
  fbrglm.
- **tidymodels** — specifically the **parsnip**, **workflows**,
  **recipes**, and **hardhat** packages [@parsnip; @workflows;
  @recipes; @hardhat] — offers a composable, framework-grade
  modelling pipeline in which `glmnet` is one of many engines and
  preprocessing is handled by hardhat / recipes.
- **broom** [@broom] adds a tidy-output layer over many model objects
  including `glmnet`. It is complementary to fbrglm rather than
  overlapping.
- **caret** is mentioned for completeness as the previous generation
  modelling framework; tidymodels effectively supersedes it in this
  space.

Table 1 summarises the comparison along the dimensions most relevant
to the manuscript's argument. All entries describe the package's
public API surface, not internals.

```{r table-related, echo = FALSE}
rel_df <- data.frame(
    package     = c("stats::glm", "glmnet", "glmnetUtils",
                    "parsnip + workflows", "fbrglm"),
    interface   = c("formula / data", "x, y matrices",
                    "formula / data",
                    "formula or recipe via workflow",
                    "formula / data"),
    backend     = c("base R IRLS", "glmnet (CD)", "calls glmnet",
                    "engine of choice (glmnet, ...)", "calls glmnet"),
    pred_cons   = c("yes (terms)",
                    "caller responsibility",
                    "yes (model.frame stored)",
                    "yes (hardhat preprocessor)",
                    "yes (xlevels + contrasts + x_colnames)"),
    fam_breadth = c("exponential family + Cox via coxph",
                    "full glmnet family list",
                    "inherits glmnet's family list",
                    "engine-specific",
                    "full glmnet family list (Section 5)"),
    notes       = c("classical SE / p-values",
                    "matrix interface; no formula",
                    "thin formula wrapper",
                    "full modelling framework; broader scope",
                    "glm-like; no classical SE under infer='none'"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(
    rel_df, format = "html", escape = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = c("package", "interface", "backend",
                  "prediction consistency", "family breadth",
                  "notes"),
    align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "l", "l"),
    caption = "Table 1: Related software in the regularized GLM space."
)
```

fbrglm differs from each of these in scope rather than in direction.
It is a single-purpose, `glm()`-like wrapper around `glmnet`, not a
modelling framework: there is no preprocessing graph, no tuning
vocabulary, no engine abstraction layer to maintain. Compared to
`glmnetUtils`, fbrglm makes the prediction-time design-matrix
alignment explicit (xlevels / contrasts / x_colnames on the fit, plus
a single helper that pads missing one-hot columns), reports
complete-case filtering through `nobs_info`, surfaces rank diagnostics
through `rank_info`, and exposes the underlying engine objects through
`as_glmnet()` / `as_cv_glmnet()`. Compared to the tidymodels stack,
fbrglm sits well below the level of recipes and tuning grids: its
target user is the practitioner who would otherwise reach for
`glmnet()` plus a private `model.matrix()` helper.

# Design and implementation

## High-level architecture

A fitted `fbrglm` object is a list of class
`c("fbrglm", "regularized_glm")` carrying, among other fields:

- `terms`, `xlevels`, `contrasts`, `x_colnames`, `x_train` — everything
  needed to rebuild a model matrix consistent with the training fit;
- `family` (the value passed to glmnet — character string or family
  object) and `family_name` (a short display string);
- `fit` (the underlying `glmnet` object) and `cv_fit` (`cv.glmnet`, or
  `NULL` for `lambda = "fix"`);
- `coefficients`, `nonzero`, `lambda_value`, `lambda_rule`;
- `nobs_info` (`n_total` / `n_dropped_missing` / `n_used`);
- `rank_info` (`rank` / `ncol` / `rank_deficient` / `pivot`);
- `weights`, `offset`, `infer`, `selection_frac`, `alpha`, `call`,
  `formula`.

The `fbrglm()` entry point mirrors `stats::glm()`:

```r
fbrglm(
    formula, data,
    family = c("gaussian", "binomial", "poisson"),
    weights = NULL, offset = NULL,
    infer  = c("none", "split", "selective"),
    selection_frac = 0.2,
    alpha = 1,
    lambda = c("cv_min", "cv_1se", "fix"),
    lambda_value = NULL,
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    ...
)
```

Arguments not native to `glmnet` (`infer`, `selection_frac`) are
recognised but only `infer = "none"` is implemented. Extra arguments
travel through `...` to `glmnet::glmnet()` / `glmnet::cv.glmnet()`.

## Algorithm 1: fitting

The fit path is straightforward. The only subtleties are the
intercept-column removal (because `glmnet` carries its own intercept)
and the storage of the design-matrix recipe alongside the fit.

```
Algorithm 1: fbrglm() fit
-----------------------------------------------------------
Input : formula, data, family, lambda rule, lambda_value,
        weights, offset, alpha
Output: an fbrglm object

  1. validate family (character or family object); validate
     lambda rule; validate infer == "none"
  2. mf  <- model.frame(formula, data, weights, offset,
                        na.action = na.omit, drop.unused.levels = TRUE)
  3. Terms     <- attr(mf, "terms")
  4. y         <- model.response(mf)
  5. w         <- model.weights(mf)  ; o <- model.offset(mf)
  6. X_full    <- model.matrix(Terms, mf)
  7. xlevels   <- saved factor levels of mf
  8. contrasts <- attr(X_full, "contrasts")
  9. X         <- X_full with the (Intercept) column removed
 10. compute rank_info via qr(X); warn if rank-deficient
 11. if lambda == "fix":
         fit    <- glmnet(X, y, family = family,
                           lambda = lambda_value, alpha, ...)
         cv_fit <- NULL
         chosen <- lambda_value
     else:
         cv_fit <- cv.glmnet(X, y, family = family, alpha, ...)
         fit    <- cv_fit$glmnet.fit
         chosen <- cv_fit$lambda.min or $lambda.1se
 12. coefs   <- coef(fit, s = chosen)
 13. nobs_info <- (n_total, n_dropped_missing, n_used)
 14. return list with class c("fbrglm","regularized_glm") containing
     Terms, xlevels, contrasts, x_colnames=colnames(X), x_train=X,
     fit, cv_fit, coefs, chosen, family, family_name,
     nobs_info, rank_info, call, formula, weights, offset,
     alpha, lambda_rule, infer, selection_frac
```

## Algorithm 2: predicting

The prediction path is the load-bearing part of the package. The
critical step is the **column alignment**: re-encoding `newdata` will
in general give a matrix with different columns than the training
matrix, and the difference is exactly what causes the
out-of-the-box failures Section 2.2 demonstrated. The helper
`.fbrglm_align_x()` does three things: pad missing columns with zeros,
drop extra columns, reorder.

```
Algorithm 2: predict.fbrglm() with newdata
-----------------------------------------------------------
Input : fbrglm object, newdata, type in {link, response, class},
        newoffset
Output: a numeric vector or matrix of predictions

  1. if newdata is NULL:
         X <- object$x_train
     else:
         Terms <- delete.response(object$terms)
         mf    <- model.frame(Terms, newdata, xlev = object$xlevels)
         X_full<- model.matrix(Terms, mf,
                               contrasts.arg = object$contrasts)
         X     <- X_full with (Intercept) column removed
         X     <- align_x(X, target = object$x_colnames):
                    - any missing target column -> add zeros
                    - any extra column           -> drop
                    - reorder to target order
  2. if type == "class":
         if family not in {binomial, multinomial}: error
         if family == "binomial":
             prob <- predict(fit, newx=X, s=chosen, type="response")
             return as.numeric(prob >= 0.5)
         else (multinomial):
             return as.vector(predict(fit, newx=X, s=chosen,
                                      type="class"))
  3. forward newoffset if appropriate:
         if model has offset and newdata is NULL: reuse object$offset
         if model has offset and newdata != NULL: require newoffset
         if length(newoffset) != nrow(X): error
  4. pred <- predict(fit, newx=X, s=chosen, type=type [,newoffset])
  5. if dim(pred) == (n,k,1): collapse to (n,k) matrix
     if dim(pred) == (n,1):   collapse to length-n vector
  6. return pred
```

Step 5 lets a single code path support both single-response families
(gaussian / binomial / poisson / Gamma / NB / Cox) and the
multi-response cases (multinomial / mgaussian), whose `predict` output
is a 3D array `(n, k, n_lambda)` from `glmnet`.

## λ-selection rules

`lambda = "cv_min"` and `"cv_1se"` go through `glmnet::cv.glmnet()`;
`"fix"` skips CV and goes through
`glmnet::glmnet(lambda = lambda_value)`. The numeric λ actually used
is always recorded in `fit$lambda_value`, and downstream methods
(`predict()`, `coef()`, `summary()`) consult that single field — there
is no second path that re-derives a λ choice elsewhere in the object.

## `nobs_info` and `rank_info`

Complete-case filtering happens via
`model.frame(..., na.action = na.omit)`, with the dropped count
surfaced both as a one-line message and as the `nobs_info` triple.
Rank deficiency is detected with `qr(X)` and recorded in
`rank_info$rank_deficient`; rank-deficient columns are **not** dropped
in the current implementation (a warning is emitted instead).
Automatic dropping via QR pivoting is on the roadmap.

## `as_glmnet()` / `as_cv_glmnet()`

These accessors expose the underlying `glmnet` / `cv.glmnet` objects
so that callers can fall back to any `glmnet`-specific tooling
without unwrapping the fbrglm object by hand. For example, plotting
the CV curve is just `plot(as_cv_glmnet(fit))`, and any third-party
package that consumes `glmnet` objects (a tidy-output layer, a
diagnostic helper, a tuning routine) keeps working unchanged.

## Design trade-offs

A handful of design decisions are load-bearing enough to be worth
articulating explicitly.

**Constant overhead in exchange for prediction safety.** The
formula-parsing pass, the storage of `terms` / `xlevels` /
`contrasts` / `x_colnames` on the object, and the alignment helper
at predict time all add a small constant cost over raw `glmnet`. The
runtime benchmark in Section 8 puts this at roughly 2–3× the
raw-`glmnet` cost on small data, in the same regime as `glmnetUtils`
and well below the tidymodels stack. The overhead is the price of
the prediction-time guarantees in Section 4.2.

**Supported vs. experimental family status.** Gaussian, binomial,
and Poisson are tested end-to-end with worked examples in this
paper, the package vignette, and the family-wide parity sweep, and
are flagged simply as *supported*. Gamma and fixed-θ negative
binomial flow through glmnet's family-object route and are also
*supported*. The Cox, multinomial, and mgaussian paths are
*experimental*: the basic fit / predict combinations work and are
covered by tests, but unusual configurations (Cox strata, Cox tie
handling beyond glmnet's defaults, multinomial grouped vs ungrouped
penalty, time-varying covariates) have not been exhaustively
validated. The package surfaces the status mismatch through
documentation rather than through silently restricting behaviour.

**Statistical honesty over UX consistency.** Refusing to produce
classical SE / z / p / CI under `infer = "none"` makes the
`summary()` output less rich than `summary.glm()`. We accept that
trade because the alternative — reporting IRLS-style quantities for
a regularized estimator without any post-selection correction —
would mislead users into using the numbers the way they use glm()
output. Honest inference is the next milestone, not the current
one.

**`glmnet` objects remain reachable.** `as_glmnet()` and
`as_cv_glmnet()` are first-class accessors. A user who needs a
glmnet-specific facility (a third-party diagnostic, a tuning helper,
a different prediction type) is one accessor call away from the
underlying object. fbrglm wraps `glmnet` rather than hiding it.

## Family argument handling

The `family` argument accepts the same shapes `glmnet` itself
accepts:

- the six character strings `"gaussian"`, `"binomial"`, `"poisson"`,
  `"cox"`, `"multinomial"`, `"mgaussian"`;
- any GLM family object (e.g. `stats::Gamma(link = "log")`,
  `MASS::negative.binomial(theta = ...)`);
- a bare family generator (e.g. `binomial`) — fbrglm calls it to get
  a family object.

The value passed to `glmnet` is stored verbatim on the fit as
`object$family`; a short display string is computed and stored as
`object$family_name`. The two are used in different places:
`family_name` drives dispatch (e.g. "is this binomial?"), and
`family` is what is fed back into `glmnet` when refits are needed.
Unknown character strings produce a helpful error referencing the six
known names; arbitrary functions that do not return family objects
are rejected at the call site rather than at `glmnet` time.

# Family support

Table 2 summarises which families are currently in scope, with their
implementation status, response shape, prediction-output shape, and
the most important caveat per row.

```{r table-families, echo = FALSE}
fam_support <- data.frame(
    model = c("Linear regression",
              "Logistic regression",
              "Poisson regression",
              "Gamma regression",
              "Negative binomial (fixed theta)",
              "Cox regression (native)",
              "Multinomial regression",
              "Multi-response Gaussian"),
    family = c('"gaussian"', '"binomial"', '"poisson"',
                "stats::Gamma(link='log')",
                "MASS::negative.binomial(theta=...)",
                '"cox" + Surv(time,status) ~ ...',
                '"multinomial"',
                '"mgaussian" + cbind(y1, y2) ~ ...'),
    response = c("continuous", "binary (0/1)", "count",
                 "positive continuous", "overdispersed count",
                 "Surv object", "multiclass factor",
                 "numeric matrix"),
    output   = c("vector", "vector / class label",
                 "vector", "vector", "vector",
                 "vector (link or response on the relative-risk scale)",
                 "(n x k) matrix or class labels",
                 "(n x q) matrix"),
    status   = c("supported", "supported", "supported",
                 "supported (family object)",
                 "supported (fixed theta only)",
                 "supported (experimental)",
                 "supported (experimental)",
                 "supported (experimental)"),
    caveat   = c("",
                 "",
                 "offsets supported via `offset=` / `newoffset=`",
                 "family object route through glmnet",
                 "theta estimation a la MASS::glm.nb is out of scope",
                 "no baseline-hazard estimation; strata / ties not fully validated",
                 "coef() returns a list (one matrix per class)",
                 "coef() returns a list (one matrix per response)"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(
    fam_support, format = "html", escape = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = c("model", "family argument", "response", "predict output",
                  "status", "caveat"),
    align = c("l", "l", "l", "l", "l", "l"),
    caption = "Table 2: Family argument forms accepted by fbrglm and their status."
)
```

The piecewise exponential survival model that the `fbrglm-families`
vignette walks through is *not* in this table because it is not a new
family: it is a Poisson regression on long-format data, fit with
`family = "poisson"` and `offset(log(exposure))`. It is closely related
to Cox regression at the population level when the intervals are fine
enough but the parameters and likelihoods are different from glmnet's
partial-likelihood Cox route.

# Worked examples

The examples below are all small, deterministic, and runnable. They
cover one model from each row of Table 2.

## Linear regression

```{r ex-gaussian}
library(fbrglm)
set.seed(101)
n <- 150
dat <- data.frame(
    y  = 0.5 + 0.8 * rnorm(n) - 0.3 * rnorm(n) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5),
    x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n)
)
fit_lm <- fbrglm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat,
                 family = "gaussian",
                 lambda = "fix", lambda_value = 0.05)
coef(fit_lm)
```

## Logistic regression with a narrowed test factor

```{r ex-binomial}
set.seed(102)
train <- data.frame(
    y  = rbinom(200, 1, 0.5),
    x1 = rnorm(200),
    g  = factor(sample(c("A","B","C"), 200, replace = TRUE),
                levels = c("A","B","C"))
)
fit_b <- fbrglm(y ~ x1 + g, data = train, family = "binomial",
                lambda = "fix", lambda_value = 0.05)
test <- data.frame(
    x1 = rnorm(5),
    g  = factor(rep(c("A","B"), length.out = 5),
                levels = c("A","B"))   # narrowed
)
head(predict(fit_b, newdata = test, type = "response"))
head(predict(fit_b, newdata = test, type = "class"))
```

The `predict()` call succeeds despite the narrowed factor levels;
`fit_b`'s `x_colnames` includes `gB` and `gC`, and the alignment
helper pads `gC` with zeros for the test rows. Unseen factor values
remain hard errors at `model.frame()` time.

## Poisson regression with an offset

```{r ex-poisson}
set.seed(103)
n <- 200
exposure <- runif(n, 0.5, 2)
x1 <- rnorm(n); x2 <- rnorm(n)
rate <- exp(-1 + 0.4 * x1 - 0.2 * x2)
dat_p <- data.frame(y  = rpois(n, rate * exposure),
                    x1 = x1, x2 = x2, exposure = exposure)
fit_p <- fbrglm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat_p, family = "poisson",
                offset = log(dat_p$exposure),
                lambda = "fix", lambda_value = 0.05)
new_dat <- dat_p[1:5, ]
predict(fit_p, newdata = new_dat,
        newoffset = log(new_dat$exposure), type = "response")
```

## Gamma regression via a family object

```{r ex-gamma}
set.seed(106)
n <- 150
x1 <- rnorm(n); x2 <- rnorm(n)
eta <- 0.4 * x1 - 0.2 * x2
dat_g <- data.frame(y  = rgamma(n, shape = 2, rate = exp(-eta)),
                    x1 = x1, x2 = x2)
fit_g <- fbrglm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat_g,
                family = stats::Gamma(link = "log"),
                lambda = "fix", lambda_value = 0.05)
fit_g$family_name
head(predict(fit_g, type = "response"))
```

## Negative binomial regression (fixed θ)

```{r ex-negbin, message = FALSE, eval = requireNamespace("MASS", quietly = TRUE)}
set.seed(107)
n <- 150
x1 <- rnorm(n); x2 <- rnorm(n)
mu <- exp(0.4 * x1 - 0.2 * x2)
dat_nb <- data.frame(y = rnbinom(n, mu = mu, size = 2),
                     x1 = x1, x2 = x2)
fit_nb <- fbrglm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat_nb,
                 family = MASS::negative.binomial(theta = 2),
                 lambda = "fix", lambda_value = 0.05)
fit_nb$family_name
head(predict(fit_nb, type = "response"))
```

Joint estimation of θ in the spirit of `MASS::glm.nb()` is *not*
implemented; θ must be chosen externally.

## Native Cox regression

```{r ex-cox, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, eval = requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)}
set.seed(105)
n <- 200
x1 <- rnorm(n); x2 <- rnorm(n)
T_event <- rexp(n, exp(0.4 * x1 - 0.2 * x2))
t_obs   <- pmin(T_event, 3)
delta   <- as.integer(T_event <= 3)
dat_cox <- data.frame(t_obs = t_obs, delta = delta,
                      x1 = x1, x2 = x2)
fit_cox <- fbrglm(survival::Surv(t_obs, delta) ~ x1 + x2,
                  data = dat_cox, family = "cox",
                  lambda = "fix", lambda_value = 0.05)
head(predict(fit_cox, type = "link"))
```

The prediction is on the linear-predictor / relative-risk scale.
fbrglm does not estimate the baseline hazard; absolute survival
curves require a separate baseline-hazard step.

## Multinomial regression

```{r ex-multinomial}
set.seed(108)
n <- 200
dat_m <- data.frame(
    y  = factor(sample(c("a","b","c"), n, replace = TRUE)),
    x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n)
)
fit_m <- fbrglm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat_m, family = "multinomial",
                lambda = "fix", lambda_value = 0.05)
dim(predict(fit_m, type = "response"))
head(predict(fit_m, type = "class"))
```

`coef(fit_m)` is a list of (sparse) matrices, one per class — matching
glmnet's own behaviour.

## Multi-response Gaussian

```{r ex-mgaussian}
set.seed(109)
n <- 150
dat_mg <- data.frame(
    y1 = rnorm(n), y2 = rnorm(n),
    x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n)
)
fit_mg <- fbrglm(cbind(y1, y2) ~ x1 + x2, data = dat_mg,
                 family = "mgaussian",
                 lambda = "fix", lambda_value = 0.05)
dim(predict(fit_mg, type = "response"))
```

## Calling glm-style methods on an fbrglm object

The S3 methods registered by fbrglm mirror the `glm()` surface most
applied users actually reach for. Using the gaussian fit from
Section 6.1:

```{r ex-glm-methods}
print(fit_lm)
```

`print()` reports the call, the resolved family / λ rule / λ value,
the complete-case bookkeeping triple, and the number of non-zero
coefficients. `summary()` returns a structured summary list whose
`print()` lays the same information out in a slightly more verbose
form, including the full coefficient vector with zeros included:

```{r ex-glm-summary, results = "hold"}
s <- summary(fit_lm)
s$family; s$lambda_method; s$lambda_value
s$nobs_info
length(s$nonzero)
```

`coef()` returns the named coefficient vector (a list for
multinomial / mgaussian); `nobs()` returns the post-filter sample
size used by the fit:

```{r ex-glm-coef-nobs}
coef(fit_lm)
nobs(fit_lm)
```

Finally, `as_glmnet(fit_lm)` and `as_cv_glmnet(fit_lm)` return the
underlying `glmnet` and `cv.glmnet` objects (the latter is `NULL`
when `lambda = "fix"`), so that any function that consumes a glmnet
object directly continues to work:

```{r ex-glm-accessors}
class(as_glmnet(fit_lm))
as_cv_glmnet(fit_lm)
```

# Benchmark design

The benchmark suite that supports the empirical claims in this paper
lives in the companion repository
[`fbrglm-experiments`](https://github.com/dsc-chiba-u/fbrglm-experiments).
It deliberately stays small, fixed-λ, and synthetic: the goal is to
make every claim reproducible in seconds on a single laptop, not to
litigate large-scale predictive performance.

## What the benchmark does and does not show

The benchmark is scoped to three questions:

1. does each method preserve the prediction-time design-matrix
   contract when training and test factor levels disagree?
2. how much constant-factor overhead does each method add at fit and
   predict time on small data?
3. does fbrglm reproduce raw `glmnet`'s predictions when both are
   given the same data and the same λ?

It does **not** attempt to compare predictive performance (no hold-out
loss is reported), and it does **not** sweep hyperparameters; every
method is run at the same fixed λ on identical inputs. Broader claims
("which package is faster overall", "which package generalises
better") would require a larger, hold-out-driven study and are out of
scope here. The numbers reported below were collected with R 4.5.3 on
Linux; exact package versions are pinned in the companion
repository's `environment.yml`.

## The three benchmark scripts

- `scripts/10_benchmark_prediction_failures.R` — constructs train and
  test data with a deliberate factor-level mismatch and records which
  methods fail and how, with one row per method.
- `scripts/11_benchmark_runtime_small.R` — measures fit + predict
  wall-clock on a small grid of `(n, p_numeric, n_factor, n_levels)`
  combinations, with five iterations per cell via `bench::mark()`.
- `scripts/12_benchmark_families_small.R` — sweeps across the eight
  `glmnet`-compatible families and records fit success, runtime, and
  the maximum absolute difference between fbrglm's prediction and a
  hand-built raw `glmnet` call on the same data.

`scripts/20_plot_small_benchmarks.R` produces the figures and
`scripts/30_make_manuscript_tables.R` produces the paste-ready
summary tables that the next section reads.

# Results

## Prediction consistency under factor-level mismatch

Factor-level mismatches between training and prediction data come in
two directions, and a wrapper that aims for `glm()`-strict semantics
needs to handle both. We probe each method on two binomial datasets.

**Scenario A — narrowed test (Table 3a).** Training has factor `g`
with levels `A / B / C / D`; the test factor is constructed with the
narrower level set `A / B`. The "missing" levels just do not appear
in the test data; the right behaviour is to produce a design matrix
of the same width as training, zero-filling the dummy columns for the
absent levels.

```{r prediction-table-narrowed, echo = FALSE}
pred_df <- utils::read.csv(
    file.path(exp_dir, "results", "summary",  # nolint
              "manuscript_prediction_table.csv"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
short_note_a <- c(
    "fbrglm"           = "default path: auto-aligns",
    "glmnet_raw_naive" = "column-width mismatch",
    "glmnet_raw_safe"  = "manual re-level required",
    "glmnetUtils"      = "default fast path fails",
    "glmnetUtils_mf"   = "user must set use.model.frame=TRUE",
    "parsnip_workflow" = "hardhat preprocessor"
)
pred_show <- data.frame(
    method = pred_df$method,
    result = pred_df$prediction_under_narrowed_factor_levels,
    burden = pred_df$user_burden,
    note   = unname(short_note_a[pred_df$method]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(pred_show) <- NULL
knitr::kable(
    pred_show, format = "html", escape = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = c("method", "result", "burden", "note"),
    align = c("l", "l", "l", "l"),
    caption = "Table 3a: Behaviour at predict time when the test factor is *narrower* than training (train: A/B/C/D, test: A/B)."
)
```

Both `Failure` rows in Table 3a produce a `glmnet` runtime error of
the form *"The number of variables in newx must be N"*. `glmnetUtils`
provides an opt-in escape: passing `use.model.frame = TRUE` switches
the wrapper to a path that builds a model frame and carries `xlevels`
forward, so the narrowed test succeeds. `fbrglm`, the workflow path,
and `glmnetUtils` with the model-frame option all succeed
automatically; raw `glmnet` succeeds only when the caller manually
re-levels the test factor before calling `model.matrix()`.

**Scenario B — novel test levels (Table 3b).** The dataset is
flipped: training has factor `g` with levels `A / B`, the test
factor with `A / B / C / D`. Now the test carries values the trained
model has never seen. The reference behaviour for this case is
`stats::predict.glm()`'s error message *"factor g has new levels
C, D"*; any wrapper claiming `glm()`-strict semantics should reproduce
it on its default path.

```{r prediction-table-novel, echo = FALSE}
pred_novel_df <- utils::read.csv(
    file.path(exp_dir, "results", "summary",  # nolint
              "manuscript_prediction_table_novel.csv"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
short_note_b <- c(
    "fbrglm"           = "default: glm-strict error",
    "fbrglm_na"        = "opt-in: rows -> NA + warning",
    "glmnet_raw_naive" = "raw column-width error",
    "glmnetUtils"      = "raw column-width error",
    "glmnetUtils_mf"   = "glm-style error (matches glm())",
    "parsnip_workflow" = "warns, silently uses reference",
    "base_glm"         = "reference (stats::predict.glm)"
)
pred_novel_show <- data.frame(
    method = pred_novel_df$method,
    result = pred_novel_df$prediction_under_novel_factor_levels,
    burden = pred_novel_df$user_burden,
    note   = unname(short_note_b[pred_novel_df$method]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(pred_novel_show) <- NULL
knitr::kable(
    pred_novel_show, format = "html", escape = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = c("method", "result", "burden", "note"),
    align = c("l", "l", "l", "l"),
    caption = "Table 3b: Behaviour at predict time when the test factor carries *novel* levels not seen in training (train: A/B, test: A/B/C/D)."
)
```

Three distinct response shapes appear in Table 3b. `fbrglm`'s default
and `glmnetUtils` with `use.model.frame = TRUE` both reproduce
`predict.glm()`'s error verbatim — that is the safe-by-default
behaviour `glm()` users expect. The default `glmnetUtils` path and a
naive `glmnet` user instead get a low-level *"number of variables in
newx"* error: the same outcome, but a less informative diagnostic.
The `parsnip` / `workflows` path takes a softer route: it warns about
the novel levels, silently coerces those cells to the reference level
in the design matrix, and returns finite predictions for every row —
which is convenient for pipeline robustness but can hide a real
covariate shift from the analyst. Finally, `fbrglm` exposes
`predict(fit, newdata, on_new_levels = "na")` for production
pipelines that need a single batch to survive an unseen level: rows
with novel levels are returned as `NA`, every other row scores
normally, and a warning names the count of dropped rows. The default
remains `"error"`, so the safety-by-default `glm()` story is
preserved unchanged.

## Runtime overhead of formula / data handling

Fit + predict wall-clock on a small grid of `(n, p_numeric, n_factor,
n_levels)` combinations, fixed λ = 0.05, median of 5 iterations from
`bench::mark()`. The compact summary in Table 4 reports
`glmnet_raw`'s median in milliseconds and the per-scenario ratio of
each other method's median to it; values larger than 1× are slower
than raw `glmnet`.

```{r runtime-table, echo = FALSE}
rt_df <- utils::read.csv(
    file.path(exp_dir, "results", "summary",  # nolint
              "manuscript_runtime_table.csv"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
scn_order <- unique(rt_df$scenario)
pick <- function(scn, mthd, col) {
    rt_df[[col]][rt_df$scenario == scn & rt_df$method == mthd]
}
rt_wide <- do.call(rbind, lapply(scn_order, function(scn) {
    data.frame(
        scenario      = scn,
        raw_ms        = sprintf("%.1f", pick(scn, "glmnet_raw",       "median_ms")),
        fbrglm        = sprintf("%.2fx", pick(scn, "fbrglm",          "relative_to_raw_glmnet")),
        glmnetUtils   = sprintf("%.2fx", pick(scn, "glmnetUtils",     "relative_to_raw_glmnet")),
        parsnip       = sprintf("%.2fx", pick(scn, "parsnip_workflow","relative_to_raw_glmnet")),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
}))
knitr::kable(
    rt_wide, format = "html", escape = TRUE,
    col.names = c("scenario", "glmnet_raw (ms)",
                  "fbrglm (× over raw)",
                  "glmnetUtils (× over raw)",
                  "parsnip_workflow (× over raw)"),
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
    caption = "Table 4: Runtime ratios across scenarios."
)
```

Method roles, repeated across scenarios: `glmnet_raw` is the fastest
matrix API; `fbrglm` is a lightweight formula interface; `glmnetUtils`
is a formula interface; `parsnip_workflow` is a full workflow
framework. Full per-iteration and per-method rows live in
`results/raw/runtime_small_raw.csv` and
`results/summary/runtime_small.csv` of the experiments repo.

![Runtime benchmark across four scenarios; bars are median of five iterations from `bench::mark()`. This is a small benchmark, not a universal performance claim.](../../fbrglm-experiments/results/figures/runtime_small.png)

The differences in this small benchmark line up with what each
method is actually doing: raw `glmnet` is the fastest because it
receives an already-built matrix and skips formula parsing; fbrglm
adds the formula-parsing pass plus the prediction-time alignment
helper; `glmnetUtils` is in a similar regime to fbrglm; the
`parsnip` / `workflows` path adds the broader workflow-framework
machinery on every call. The relevant takeaway is therefore that
fbrglm occupies a lightweight middle ground — *not* that fbrglm is
the fastest of the four. A "fastest" claim would require a larger
and more rigorous study.

## Family-wide prediction parity

A complementary sanity check sweeps across `glmnet`-compatible
families to verify that fbrglm's formula/data wrapper does not
silently change what `glmnet` computes. Eight families — `gaussian`,
`binomial`, `poisson`, `Gamma` (via `stats::Gamma(link = "log")`),
fixed-θ negative binomial (via
`MASS::negative.binomial(theta = ...)`), native Cox (via
`family = "cox"` with `Surv(time, status) ~ ...`), `multinomial`, and
`mgaussian` — are each fit at λ = 0.05 with both fbrglm and a
hand-built raw `glmnet` call on the same data, and the predictions
are compared (Table 5).

```{r family-table, echo = FALSE}
fam_df <- utils::read.csv(
    file.path(exp_dir, "results", "summary",  # nolint
              "manuscript_family_table.csv"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
fam_show <- fam_df[, c("family", "response", "fbrglm_vs_glmnet",
                        "fbrglm_runtime_ms", "raw_glmnet_runtime_ms",
                        "note")]
knitr::kable(
    fam_show, format = "html", escape = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = c("family", "response", "fbrglm vs raw",
                  "fbrglm (ms)", "raw (ms)", "note"),
    align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "l"),
    caption = "Table 5: Family-wide parity sweep between fbrglm and raw glmnet."
)
```

The maximum absolute difference between fbrglm's prediction and the
raw `glmnet` prediction is zero for every family in the table: the
wrapper changes the user-facing interface and the prediction-time
design-matrix handling, but not the optimisation. Two qualifications
go with the table: the negative binomial entry uses *fixed* θ
(joint θ estimation in the spirit of `MASS::glm.nb()` is out of
scope), and the Cox entry exercises glmnet's native
partial-likelihood Cox route — distinct from the *piecewise
exponential Poisson* survival formulation walked through in the
`fbrglm-families` package vignette. `glmnetUtils` is the other
formula-based interface that succeeded on all eight families; the
`parsnip` / `workflows` pipeline succeeded on the three families with
a same-engine equivalent in core parsnip (`gaussian`, `binomial`,
`multinomial`) and is recorded as "not attempted" elsewhere rather
than as a failure.

# Replication material

The benchmark numbers, figures, and manuscript tables can be
reproduced from a fresh checkout of
<https://github.com/dsc-chiba-u/fbrglm-experiments>. Path resolution
inside the scripts has three priorities — the `FBRGLM_EXP_ROOT`
environment variable, the current working directory if it contains
`environment.yml` and an `R/` subdirectory, and a development-time
fallback — so the same scripts run from any checkout location.

```sh
# from the experiments repository root
conda env create -f environment.yml          # first time only
conda activate fbrglm-dev

Rscript scripts/run_all_smoke.R              # 00–05 sanity checks
Rscript scripts/run_all_benchmarks_small.R   # 10, 11, 12
Rscript scripts/20_plot_small_benchmarks.R   # PNGs
Rscript scripts/30_make_manuscript_tables.R  # CSVs and MD tables
```

The pipeline produces:

- `results/summary/families_small.csv` and
  `results/raw/families_small_raw.csv` — per (family, method) parity.
- `results/summary/prediction_failures_small.csv` and
  `results/summary/runtime_small.csv` — small-benchmark summaries.
- `results/raw/runtime_small_raw.csv` — per-iteration timings.
- `results/summary/manuscript_prediction_table.{csv,md}`,
  `results/summary/manuscript_runtime_table.{csv,md}`,
  `results/summary/manuscript_family_table.{csv,md}` — the three
  paste-ready summaries referenced in this paper.
- `results/figures/prediction_failures_small.png` and
  `results/figures/runtime_small.png` — figures.

The package source for fbrglm itself lives at
<https://github.com/dsc-chiba-u/fbrglm>. `R CMD check --as-cran` is
clean modulo the routine `New submission` and `unable to verify
current time` NOTEs. Two vignettes ship with the package:
`vignette("fbrglm")` (a tour of the formula/data interface, the
`nobs_info` triple, factor narrowing, and offsets) and
`vignette("fbrglm-families")` (the family-by-family worked examples
of Section 6, plus the piecewise exponential survival example).

# Limitations and future work

The MVP is deliberately narrow. The roadmap items below are tracked
in the package `TODO.md`.

- **Honest inference.** Only `infer = "none"` is implemented.
  `infer = "split"` (data splitting with `selection_frac`) and
  `infer = "selective"` [@tibshirani2016selective] are the next two
  inference modes. No
  classical SE / z / p / CI is produced; doing so naively for a
  regularized estimator would be misleading.
- **Negative binomial θ.** Fixed-θ NB works via the family object
  route. Joint θ estimation in the spirit of `MASS::glm.nb()` is a
  separate optimisation problem (alternating between coefficient and
  θ updates plus a separate likelihood for θ) and is out of scope.
- **Cox extensions.** The native Cox path is exercised by tests for
  the standard `Surv(time, status) ~ ...` setup, but Cox strata, tie
  handling beyond glmnet's defaults, and time-varying covariates
  have not been validated and should be considered untested
  territory in fbrglm. Falling back to `as_glmnet(fit_cox)` gives
  the user direct access to `coxnet` for these cases.
- **x / y direct entry.** The `x` and `y` arguments are reserved
  but not yet implemented; supply `formula` + `data`.
- **Rank-deficient designs.** Detected via `qr()` and reported on
  `rank_info$rank_deficient` plus a warning, but offending columns
  are not yet dropped automatically. QR-pivot column dropping is on
  the roadmap.
- **Benchmark scope.** The benchmarks in Section 8 are small,
  synthetic, and at a fixed λ. They are sanity checks, not general
  performance claims; in particular no claim of universal runtime
  superiority is supported by these data.
- **Submission format.** This draft renders to `html_document`
  because a LaTeX engine is not present in the local environment.
  The YAML metadata is already in JSS structure; flipping the
  `output:` block to `rticles::jss_article` and installing a LaTeX
  distribution will produce the JSS PDF form from the same source.

# Conclusion

fbrglm is best understood as a practical API layer over `glmnet`
rather than as a new modelling system. Its contribution is to make
formula-based regularized GLM workflows safer and more reproducible —
specifically, to keep the prediction-time design matrix consistent
with the fit-time design matrix by default, to surface the diagnostic
information that calling code routinely needs (missing-row counts,
rank status, the underlying `glmnet` objects), and to do so across
the same set of families `glmnet` itself accepts. Three concrete
contributions:

1. a `glm()`-like formula / data interface to `glmnet` covering
   character family strings and arbitrary GLM family objects;
2. prediction-time design-matrix consistency via stored `xlevels`,
   `contrasts`, and `x_colnames`, with zero-padding of any missing
   one-hot column at predict time;
3. parity with raw `glmnet` predictions in the family-wide sweep —
   `max |Δ| = 0` for every one of the eight glmnet-compatible
   families tested.

The empirical claim from the small benchmark is intentionally modest:
fbrglm introduces a small constant overhead over raw `glmnet` in the
tested setting, is comparable to `glmnetUtils`, and remains
substantially lighter than the `parsnip` / `workflows` path. The
family-wide parity check confirms that the wrapper changes the user
interface but not the optimisation. Whether richer inference modes —
data splitting and selective inference — and broader validation of
the experimental family paths (Cox extensions in particular) can be
added without losing this simplicity is the central question of the
next milestone.
